title: Twenty First Word First Station Conclusion Worldly Deception Death And The Grave

questions.question: What main warning is given in this passage?
questions.answer: A person should not be fooled by loving only this world and forgetting the hereafter.

questions.question: Which Qur’an idea is mentioned about the life of this world?
questions.answer: The passage says that worldly things can deceive people.

questions.question: What kind of person is being spoken to in the passage?
questions.answer: It speaks to a careless self that enjoys this life too much and neglects the next life.

questions.question: What animal is used in the comparison?
questions.answer: An ostrich.

questions.question: Why is the ostrich unable to escape the hunter in the example?
questions.answer: It cannot fly away.

questions.question: What does the ostrich do when it notices the hunter?
questions.answer: It pushes its head into the sand.

questions.question: What problem still remains even after the ostrich hides its head?
questions.answer: Its large body is still out in the open where the hunter can see it.

questions.question: What happens to the ostrich’s own sight when its head is in the sand?
questions.answer: It cannot see the hunter anymore.

questions.question: What are readers being asked to do with this comparison?
questions.answer: They are being told to think carefully about it and take a lesson from it.

questions.question: What does the passage say about the attractions of this world?
questions.answer: They may seem nice, but they can trick people.

questions.question: What has the heedless self forgotten?
questions.answer: It has forgotten the hereafter.

questions.question: What does the heedless self mainly chase after?
questions.answer: It chases worldly life and its pleasures.

questions.question: What comparison is used to wake the person up?
questions.answer: The person is compared to an ostrich.

questions.question: In the example, what danger does the ostrich notice?
questions.answer: It notices a hunter.

questions.question: What wrong choice does the ostrich make instead of escaping?
questions.answer: It hides its head rather than dealing with the danger.

questions.question: Does hiding its head protect the ostrich’s whole body?
questions.answer: No. Its body remains exposed.

questions.question: Who can still clearly see the ostrich?
questions.answer: The hunter can still see it.

questions.question: What has changed for the ostrich after it hides its head?
questions.answer: It no longer sees the hunter, even though the danger is still there.

questions.question: What does the passage begin with after mentioning Allah’s name?
questions.answer: It begins with the idea that worldly gain is misleading.

questions.question: Is the passage giving comfort, a warning, or a funny story?
questions.answer: It is giving a warning lesson.

questions.question: What is wrong with the self being addressed?
questions.answer: It is careless, attached to this life, and forgetful of the next life.

questions.question: What creature is chosen for the example?
questions.answer: An ostrich.

questions.question: What does the ostrich understand before it hides?
questions.answer: It realizes a hunter is there.

questions.question: What important ability does the ostrich lack in the example?
questions.answer: It cannot fly away.

questions.question: What foolish action does it take?
questions.answer: It buries its head in the sand.

questions.question: What does this show about the ostrich’s thinking?
questions.answer: It acts as though hiding from its own sight will remove the danger.

questions.question: What detail shows that its plan fails?
questions.answer: Most of its body is still easy to see.

questions.question: What is the final instruction given to the self in this short passage?
questions.answer: It is told to think about the example and truly see its meaning.

questions.question: What false idea about worldly life is challenged in this passage?
questions.answer: The false idea that worldly enjoyment is enough and truly satisfying.

questions.question: What has happened to the self’s attention toward the hereafter?
questions.answer: It has been neglected and forgotten.

questions.question: What one-sided goal does the self have?
questions.answer: It wants only this world.

questions.question: What comparison makes the warning easier to understand?
questions.answer: The warning uses the picture of an ostrich and a hunter.

questions.question: In the example, what does the ostrich do because it cannot escape properly?
questions.answer: It hides its head in the sand.

questions.question: What does the ostrich hope will happen by doing that?
questions.answer: It hopes the hunter will not notice it.

questions.question: Why is that hope foolish?
questions.answer: Because the hunter can still see the bird’s uncovered body.

questions.question: What is the difference between the ostrich and the hunter in what they can see?
questions.answer: The hunter still sees the ostrich, but the ostrich no longer sees the hunter.

questions.question: What emotional condition is described in the self at the start of the passage?
questions.answer: It is deeply heedless and wrongly pleased with worldly life.

questions.question: What important part of faith is missing from this self’s focus?
questions.answer: Remembering the hereafter.

questions.question: What does the passage say worldly goods are like?
questions.answer: They are deceptive and can fool people.

questions.question: What animal picture is used to explain heedlessness?
questions.answer: An ostrich hiding from a hunter.

questions.question: What does the ostrich first become aware of?
questions.answer: It becomes aware of danger nearby.

questions.question: Why doesn’t the ostrich simply leave the scene?
questions.answer: It is unable to fly off.

questions.question: What does the ostrich choose to hide?
questions.answer: It hides only its head.

questions.question: What part stays visible and vulnerable?
questions.answer: Its body stays exposed.

questions.question: What does the ostrich gain by putting its head in the sand?
questions.answer: It only stops itself from seeing the danger.

questions.question: What does the passage say about the things of this world?
questions.answer: They can mislead people and make false promises.

questions.question: What has the self become absorbed in?
questions.answer: It has become absorbed in worldly life.

questions.question: What has this self neglected?
questions.answer: It has neglected the life to come.

questions.question: What example from nature is used in the warning?
questions.answer: The example of an ostrich facing a hunter.

questions.question: What does the ostrich notice in the story?
questions.answer: It notices someone hunting it.

questions.question: What weakness does the ostrich have in this example?
questions.answer: It cannot escape by flying.

questions.question: What action does it take because of that weakness?
questions.answer: It hides its head in the sand.

questions.question: What mistaken belief seems to guide that action?
questions.answer: It behaves as if danger is gone when it cannot see it.

questions.question: What fact proves the ostrich is still in danger?
questions.answer: Its body is still uncovered and visible.

questions.question: In a simple cause-and-effect way, what happens when the ostrich hides its head?
questions.answer: It loses sight of the hunter while the hunter still sees it.

questions.question: What warning does this give to people?
questions.answer: Looking away from a serious truth does not remove the truth.

questions.question: What is the passage asking the self to do at the end?
questions.answer: It is asking the self to reflect carefully on the comparison and learn from it.
